claims.text: Equimolar quinary metal nanoparticles can initially crystallize as a single-phase solid solution.
A near-equimolar lattice containing at least five principal elements has configurational entropy of at least 1.5R.
Increasing the number of near-equimolar principal elements increases total configurational entropy.
High configurational entropy reduces atomic mobility in equimolar quinary nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy lowers enthalpy-driven segregation.
Enhanced mixing entropy hampers phase separation in quinary metal nanoparticles.
Enhanced mixing entropy maintains a homogeneous, disordered atomic arrangement at high temperature.
Equimolar quinary nanoparticles retain a single-phase solid-solution lattice throughout 473–1923 K.
Equimolar quinary nanoparticles exhibit minimal elemental segregation throughout 473–1923 K.
The predicted structural and chemical stability persists in representative catalytic or thermoelectric operating environments.
Comparable quaternary or off-stoichiometric nanoparticles undergo phase transformation or significant chemical segregation under the same thermal conditions.
Five-element nanoparticle mixtures form a single phase more readily than binary nanoparticle mixtures under the cited synthesis conditions.
With limited free-atom mobility, increasing the number of atom types makes random-alloy formation more likely.
Exothermic pairwise interactions may overcome entropy stabilization under extreme or prolonged operating conditions.
Dominant pairwise interactions under extreme or prolonged conditions can cause partial phase separation and limit the practical operating range.
Quantitative interdiffusion barriers for the proposed nanoparticles are not established.
The temperatures at which local ordering may emerge are not established.
